text: Day after day she follows you through the forum, shouting. What she says is true, and it is terrible to hear it from her: it is not her voice.
You cannot reach them through the crowd. You can only hear it.
At Lydia’s house someone says, “Listen,” and from across the sleeping town comes the faint sound of singing.

In the morning the magistrates sent word to let them go quietly. Paul refused: they were Roman citizens, beaten in public without a trial, and the magistrates had to come and escort them out themselves (Acts 16:35–39).
Night falls. Paul and Silas are in the inner prison with their feet in the stocks. Where are you?
From the gate you hear it: two voices singing a psalm in the dark, and no one telling them to stop.
Roman prisons fed their prisoners little or nothing; friends and family brought food. Lydia’s household would have done what they could.
Someone has to bring a light. It is you. Your hands are shaking so that the lamp flame jumps on the walls.

“Why must we enter the Kingdom of God through many afflictions?” (Acts 14:22)

Through many afflictions: and at midnight in the stocks, Paul and Silas were singing. (Acts 14:22; 16:25)
Outside the prison wall you stop walking. Someone inside is singing.

Around one table in Lydia’s house: a seller of purple, a jailer and his family, and two men who cannot lean back for their wounds. This is the church in Philippi. Somewhere in the city, a slave girl knows her own voice again; Acts does not tell us what became of her.
She looks up, bewildered, like someone waking. For the first time you hear her own voice. She asks what day it is.
But when her masters saw that the hope of their gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas, and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” They spoke the word of the Lord to him, and to all who were in his house.
The jailer, being roused out of sleep and seeing the prison doors open, drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.
But about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.
She was doing this for many days. But Paul, becoming greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I charge you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her!” It came out that very hour.

The multitude rose up together against them, and the magistrates tore their clothes off of them, and commanded them to be beaten with rods. When they had laid many stripes on them, they threw them into prison, charging the jailer to keep them safely,
They went out of the prison, and entered into Lydia’s house. When they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them, and departed.
who, having received such a charge, threw them into the inner prison, and secured their feet in the stocks.
But Paul cried with a loud voice, saying, “Don’t harm yourself, for we are all here!”

He took them the same hour of the night, and washed their stripes, and was immediately baptized, he and all his household. He brought them up into his house, and set food before them, and rejoiced greatly, with all his household, having believed in God.

It happened, as we were going to prayer, that a certain girl having a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much gain by fortune telling. Following Paul and us, she cried out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to us the way of salvation!”
He called for lights and sprang in, and, fell down trembling before Paul and Silas, and brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
